newsitem.title: USA: U.S.-Canada fight over dairy, chickens far from settled.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-Canada fight over dairy, chickens far from settled.

text.p: Like the battery-powered rabbit in the TV commercial, some U.S.-Canada trade fights just seem to keep going and going and going, and the dispute over Canadian duties on U.S. dairy products and poultry seems to be one of them.

Despite a final ruling Monday by a NAFTA panel that squashed Washington's complaints against the Canadian tariff system and ruled in favour of Canada's policy, administration officials and industry representatives said the fight is far from over.

"The United States will do everything possible, consistent with our trade laws, to seek the ultimate elimination of these duties ..." said U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman and Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky in a joint statement released Monday evening after the ruling.
Industry officals said the administration's tough-sounding statement clearly indicated that Washington intends to pursue the fight, and they pledged to support those efforts.

"This is not going to go away," said Tom Suber, executive director of the U.S. Dairy Export Council. "The U.S. dairy industry will not waiver on efforts to estalish free trade with Canada, and we will not give up because of a misguided panel report."

At issue is whether Canada's high import duties on incoming U.S. dairy products and poultry are legal under the North American Free Trade Agreement. Canada imposed the tariffs, which range from 25 to 350 percent, on the products last year in place of quotas it previously had on shipments of American dairy and poultry products.

The issue could easily become embroiled in the debate next year over legislation that would give the administration authority to negotiate an expansion of NAFTA to include Chile, industry officials said.
Trade analysts believe the administration will face a tough fight in the Republican-controlled Congress to win the so-called fast track trade negotiation authority.
Officials warned not to expect any resolution soon of the contentious disagreement.

"We're somewhat pessimistic about the chances for any immediate or near-term solutions," said Christine Nelson of the United Egg Producers and United Egg Association. "Once you throw this back in negotiations it just becomes this back-and-forth volleyball that never seems to end."
Canada has claimed that its tariffs are legal under the rules of the World Trade Organisation, but the United States has insisted that NAFTA regulations forbid such duties.

The United States last year requested that a dispute settlement panel under the auspices of NAFTA be formed to settle the fight. The ruling by the panel has been closely watched, not only because of the issue at hand, but because it was the first such panel formed under the relatively new trade agreement, and could set a precedent for future disputes.

How much fire power Washington has left after its stunning defeat is unclear. Administration officials Tuesday were refusing to comment on what their next move will be, but industry sources said there are a number of options, including government-to-government negotiations.
"We would like the two governments to sit down and cooperatively look at this now," said Jerry Kozack, senior vice president of the International Dairy Foods Association.

Dairy and poultry officials said they would likely restart a coalition that was formed last year to address the issue, and said their representatives would discuss the problem with U.S. officials next week during a meeting of World Trade Organisation ministers in Singapore.
